### F-10. `hex64`

The `hex64` formula is defined as:

`hex64(x) = lowercase hexadecimal of the 8 bytes of x (two's complement, LEAST significant byte first, little-endian), exactly 16 characters; unhex64(h) accepts only 16 characters of [0-9a-f] and returns the same 8 bytes` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*

**Variables:**

| Variable | Type | Range | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `x` | 64-bit value | 0 … 2^64 − 1 (a signed GDScript int above 2^63 − 1 reads negative [UNV]) | `T`, `world_seed`, `state_hash`, per-block hashes | Any header value that can exceed 2^53 (S-1) |
| `h` | string | exactly 16 chars (32 for the 128-bit `campaign_id`) | header | Uppercase, a wrong width or a non-hex character is a refusal (`SL_PRECHECK_HEADER_HEX_MALFORMED`); there is no general string-to-int parse |

**Output Range:** a bijection between 8-byte values and 16-character strings; `unhex64(hex64(x)) = x` bit for bit for every `x`, including values a float cannot hold.

**Example:** `world_seed = 2^64 − 1` → `"ffffffffffffffff"` (the signed value is −1 [UNV]); `T = 2^53 + 1 = 9 007 199 254 740 993` → `"0100000000002000"`; `"FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF"` and `"ffffffffffffffff0"` are refused. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* **One endianness everywhere:** the H64 truncation (first 8 bytes of SHA-256, read little-endian into the integer, SL-16) and this hex form are both little-endian, so an H64 hex string is exactly the first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 digest and the byte order never flips between hashing and printing. **Fixed vectors** (value → hex): 0 → `0000000000000000`; 1 → `0100000000000000`; 2^53 + 1 → `0100000000002000`; 2^63 − 1 → `ffffffffffffff7f`; 2^63 → `0000000000000080` (the signed value is −2^63 [UNV]); 2^64 − 1 → `ffffffffffffffff`. **Implementation note:** build and parse the string from the 8 bytes (`PackedByteArray.hex_encode()` and `String.hex_decode()`, [UNV]); `String.hex_to_int` and `PackedByteArray.encode_s64` are not used for header hex, because a value of 2^63 or more reads or overflows as a negative signed integer.

content.content: **SL-10 (continued) — writer thread contract, polling and abandonment** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. *Hand-off.* The worker receives only the per-block `PackedByteArray`s (immutable, caller-owned, *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*), file paths and integers (position, generation, `write_epoch`, retry counts): no kernel reference, no block, no Node and no `Callable` that touches the scene tree, and it never calls `call_deferred` into Save/Load or waits on the main thread. It publishes a status record (`state` ∈ the T-4 write states, `write_epoch`, `generation`, `position`, result code) under a `Mutex` [UNV: the status publication pattern is confirmed by the spike]; the main thread only **polls** that record and never joins the worker, because `Thread.wait_to_finish` and `WorkerThreadPool.wait_for_task_completion` take no timeout, so a join at the `DEAD` boundary would hang the frame on a hung write and could deadlock a worker that reports back through `call_deferred` [UNV: confirmed by the spike, AC-SL-90]. *Polling.* A tick-boundary poll in `RUNNING`; a frame poll from the Save/Load Node with `process_mode = PROCESS_MODE_ALWAYS` [UNV: confirmed in `PAUSED` and `LOADING`] in `PAUSED`, `LOADING`, `SAVING` and during the quit wait, where no tick runs and a tick-boundary poll would never fire. *`DOWNED` entry.* When a bound seat enters `DOWNED` with a job in flight, the main thread sets the job's `finish_or_abort` flag in the status record: the worker completes only its required steps, takes no rename retries beyond the first, skips the manifest rewrite (a hint) and aborts at its first failure, removing its `.tmp`; the remaining work must settle within `DEATH_STUB_WRITE_WAIT_MS` of the command, measured on the monotonic millisecond source (an I/O timeout only, SL-23), else the job is abandoned at that moment. *`DEAD`.* A job still busy at the `DEAD` boundary is abandoned with no wait (SL-7). *General deadline.* A job that has not reported `WRITTEN` or `FAILED` within `WRITE_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS` of its hand-off is abandoned in any kernel state, `DOWNED` or not (`SL_WRITE_ABANDONED_TIMEOUT`, `save_status` reads `FAILED`, `fail_n` is incremented and the backoff of F-2 applies), so a worker that hangs during healthy play cannot hold the hard gate until someone dies; `DEATH_STUB_WRITE_WAIT_MS` stays the shorter limit that starts at `DOWNED` entry. *Abandon semantics.* To abandon a job the main thread increments `write_epoch`, logs `SL_WRITE_ABANDONED_AT_DEATH` (or `SL_WRITE_ABANDONED_TIMEOUT` when a deadline expired), takes the job out of `writer_busy` (an abandoned job never counts toward the hard gate, so one hung worker cannot disable every later autosave) and records its ring position as **claimed**: F-9 skips claimed positions until the job reports, and if no unclaimed position other than the newest generation's remains, the write ends `FAILED` with `SL_WRITE_NO_POSITION` and backs off. Temporary names carry `write_epoch` (`gen_<write_epoch>_<n>.tmp`), so an abandoned job's `.tmp` and a later job's can never be the same file. The worker re-reads `write_epoch` from its status record immediately before each ring-touching rename and aborts (removing its `.tmp`) if it is stale; a job that lands a generation despite that (the check-then-rename race, or a worker that resumed after being stuck past the check) reports its old `write_epoch`, and the main thread moves the file to `quarantine/` as `STALE_EPOCH`, never a candidate (SL-3). The worker is never killed. *Owner.* Capture and every `request_*` call stay on the main thread; the single Save/Load Node (SL-6, close mechanism) owns the worker handle and the poll. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* **Thread model, reaping, exit, lock.** *Model:* one `Thread` per job (no `WorkerThreadPool`), its handle held on a `RefCounted` `WriteJob` object that also carries the status record, so the thread's lifetime is the job's. *Reaping:* each poll (tick-boundary or frame) calls `wait_to_finish()` on a job whose thread reports `!is_alive()`; a job that is not alive and has published no terminal `WRITTEN` or `FAILED` status is a worker killed by a GDScript error: `SL_WRITE_WORKER_DIED`, `save_status` reads `FAILED`, `fail_n` is incremented, the ring position is released and the `.tmp` is left to T-6, instead of the 30 s `WRITE_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS` hold of the hard gate. *Cap:* at most `MAX_LIVE_ABANDONED_JOBS` (default 2) abandoned workers may be alive at once; at the cap a new write ends `FAILED` with `SL_WRITE_TOO_MANY_ABANDONED` and backs off until one reports. *Exit:* process exit never blocks on a busy or abandoned worker (no `wait_to_finish` on a live thread); a `QUIT` write that is itself busy follows SL-6's timeout, and an abandoned worker still running at exit is left to the OS, its `.tmp` handled by T-6 on the next open. *Single instance:* the campaign directory is opened under an exclusive lock (`campaign.lock`, created with an exclusive open and holding the process id; the mechanism and its behaviour under OneDrive and antivirus are [UNV], spike rows in AC-SL-30 and AC-SL-90); a second process that cannot take it opens the campaign **READ_ONLY**: it writes no generation, runs no T-6 deletion or quarantine move and offers New campaign and Quit only (AC-SL-147), because two processes would collide on `gen_` and `.tmp` names and T-6 would delete the other process's work.

content.content: **SL-23 — Determinism, save-scum and wall clock.** Every persisted counter and seed is restored exactly (the kernel's `rng_derive` with counters inside the owners' blocks, G4 and D.10; the Graph keys its random draws by `(step_no, subject_id)` from `world_seed`), so the **physical** world replays the same way (Pillar 1). Whether a **perception** draw (a false system state's onset, sanity drift) replays identically after a restore, or is re-keyed, is Sanity & Hallucination Rules' decision; Save/Load makes no promise either way, and routes the constraint that any re-keying must not be steerable by the player — no reroll oracle through quit or death (OQ-37). *(Amended 2026-10-26 — CD-GDD-ALIGN)* **Threat draws and `restore_epoch` (user ruling D16, OQ-47; OQ-49 and OQ-50 closed)** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1 as amended by R13/R14)* *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R13/R14)*: Attention and Horror re-key their threat draws per restore, while the Graph's physical failures and every persisted counter and seed replay exactly (the first sentence of this paragraph stands, AC-SL-68). Resolved 2026-10-27 — delegated ruling R1, as amended 2026-10-28 by delegated rulings R13 and R14 (user delegated all remaining calls, including naming the reference machine): **Save/Load owns `restore_epoch`**, a persisted unsigned 32-bit integer that starts at 0 at `new_game` (SL-18) and is stored in the per-slot side file `slot_epoch.bin` (SL-19), so it survives a process kill, a lost `campaign.json` and a step-back. (0) *Storage (R14).* `user://saves/<campaign_id>/slot_epoch.bin` holds 8 bytes: the u32, little-endian, followed by its CRC32. The Save/Load worker writes it atomically: `slot_epoch.tmp`, flush, rename over `slot_epoch.bin`, re-read with a valid CRC32, which is the `EPOCH_DURABLE` report. It is in no generation file, so no generation's bytes, trailer SHA-256, `state_hash` or any key derived from them (SL-12's REBASED baseline key included) ever change after `VERIFYING`. Each `WORLD` generation header records the value live when that generation was written (SL-1), a read-only recovery copy that is never rewritten. The value is read once when the campaign is opened (T-6) and held in memory (`e_mem`). (1) *Advance (R13).* A death-stub restore (`DEATH_STUB`) and a `FAULT_RECOVERY` always advance `restore_epoch`. A Continue (`LOAD_GAME`, in-process or after a fresh process start) advances it unless the generation it restores is a `QUIT` generation that is the newest non-demoted verified generation: that Continue **carries the epoch unchanged** and writes nothing, so a Save & Quit followed by Continue replays the identical threat draws (user ruling D16, "not steerable by quit", outranks R1). A Continue of any other generation (an `AUTO` or `EVENT` generation after a kill or crash, or an older generation reached by fallback) advances it. An advance sets `restore_epoch := min(2^32 − 1, max(e_mem, e_slot) + 1)`, `e_slot` the value last read from `slot_epoch.bin`; at 2^32 − 1 it saturates and logs. A step-back, a demotion, a quarantine or a lost manifest cannot lower it. A stub that finds nothing loadable (`SL_LOAD_NO_LOADABLE_SAVE`) restores nothing and does not advance it. (2) *Durable before the restore is requested (R14).* When an advance is due, Save/Load runs a pre-restore staging step: after selection, pre-check and staging (SL-8, SL-11) it computes the new value and hands the `slot_epoch.bin` write to the worker as its own job, never queued behind a generation write or an abandoned job (SL-10). It polls the job once per frame, never blocking the main thread, and calls `request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash)` only after `EPOCH_DURABLE`, so the kernel's `LOADING` holds no wait on Save/Load I/O and stays atomic within one boundary service (kernel CR-15). *Staging interval (`t_epoch_wait`, F-8).* On the death stub the kernel stays `RUNNING` from the `DEAD` boundary to the boundary at which `request_restore` is made: normally one frame, at most `RESTORE_EPOCH_WRITE_MAX_MS` (30 frames at 60 Hz). During it the seat stays `DEAD`, the hard gate is closed (a seat `DEAD`, a restore pending), and a `restore_pending` latch refuses every capture and pause request of Save/Load's (the dead world is never saved, SL-7) and answers further restore triggers with `SL_LOAD_REENTRANT`. The staged payload is immutable, so nothing ticked in the interval reaches the restored world except `PROFILE`-scoped writes (Pillar 5), and the Presenter holds the down sheet's last frame. For a Continue the staging runs behind the Continue press, before the kernel is touched; a carried Continue has no staging interval. (2a) *Failure path, a listed exposure.* If the write fails, or `RESTORE_EPOCH_WRITE_MAX_MS` (placeholder 500, a monotonic I/O timeout) passes without `EPOCH_DURABLE`, Save/Load still calls `request_restore` with the advanced value held in memory, logs `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` and sets `save_status = FAILED`, because the device is failing and saving is impossible anyway. The worker re-attempts the `slot_epoch.bin` write with the next write job, and after every later `WRITTEN` generation Save/Load rewrites `slot_epoch.bin` whenever the in-memory value is ahead of the file. A kill before a later successful write may replay that epoch once (OQ-25). (2b) *Recovery copy.* A missing `slot_epoch.bin`, or one failing its CRC32, reads as `max(the newest verified generation's header copy, 0) + 1`, logs `SL_EPOCH_FILE_REBUILT` and is rewritten by the worker; a leftover `slot_epoch.tmp` is deleted (T-6). Deleting the side file by hand therefore re-keys the next stretch once, a tampering exposure of the same class as editing any save file (OQ-25). (3) *Reach into the sim.* `request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash)` hands the value to the kernel, which exposes it read-only, sim-visible and pure in `kernel.clock` as `(T, world_seed, restore_epoch)` before the first `restore()`. The kernel owns the one derivation for threat draws, `counter_eff = rng_counter + RESTORE_KEY_STRIDE × restore_epoch` (`RESTORE_KEY_STRIDE` 1 048 576, owned by the kernel; the stream-name hash stays cached and unchanged); Attention and Horror call that derivation and define none of their own, and the name `threat_epoch()` is retired in favour of `restore_epoch`. The Graph's physical failures and every persisted counter never read it. (4) *Determinism is defined given the pair:* the same (save bytes, `restore_epoch`) replays identically, and tests pin the epoch (AC-SL-142, AC-SL-145). (5) *What it prices, stated plainly:* the player can neither pick nor predict the new value; a death re-keys the next stretch (the price, metric M2); a Save & Quit followed by Continue carries the epoch (R13), so the threat draws after it are those an uninterrupted run would meet and quit buys nothing (metric M3 measures only the disguised manual save); a kill then Continue of an `AUTO` or `EVENT` generation advances it, priced by the minutes lost since that autosave (OQ-25). A kill after a carried Continue, followed by a second Continue of the same `QUIT` generation, also carries the epoch and replays that stretch exactly, a repeat and not a re-key, an accepted exposure of the same kind as OQ-25's kill. History: the rule "advances on a death-stub restore only" and R1's rule "advances on every restore" are superseded by (1) (R13), and R1's header rewrite of the restored generation and its end-of-`LOADING` wait by (0) and (2) (R14). Save/Load stores true SIM state only (SL-24). Every interval, gap and window in SL-4, SL-5 and SL-8 is in ticks read from `kernel.clock.T`; `created_unix` and `game_version` are file metadata written by the service and never read by the sim (H9), so the tests are deterministic. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **Wall clock, and the one exception.** The wall clock is never read in a decision about sim time. `SAVE_QUIT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `RENAME_RETRY_DELAY_MS`, `READ_RETRY_DELAY_MS` and `DEATH_STUB_WRITE_WAIT_MS` are millisecond **I/O timeouts** that must run while `T` is frozen (`PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `LOADING`), so they read the engine's **monotonic** millisecond counter through an injected source; a timeout never changes sim state, schedules an autosave or enters a gate input. `RESTORE_EPOCH_WRITE_MAX_MS` is the fifth monotonic I/O timeout and the one that runs while `T` advances (the death stub's dead-world staging interval, (2)); it reads the same source and changes no sim state *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R14)*. The Graph's note that "single-slot autosave is Save/Load's and the user's decision" is answered by SL-3's ring; the determinism argument is unaffected. The kernel's `rng_derive` note that a 63-bit owner-defined key is a valid `counter` appears only in OQ-3 as a routed kernel amendment (D.10), not as a rule here. A process kill after a mistake rewinds by at most one interval plus the deferral cap — the same price as dying, minus the death floor — and is an accepted, unpreventable exposure (no write can protect against it), recorded for playtest.

# Design Document Rules

- The 8 GDD sections are: Overview, Player Fantasy, Detailed Rules, Formulas, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Tuning Knobs, Acceptance Criteria
- **How many are required depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system **defines numeric rules**: rates, curves, thresholds, costs, damage, drop weights — anything a balance pass would tune) at `standard`, none at `minimal` (the design record there is `design/game-brief.md`). - **Section-name alias**: The GDD template and `/design-system` author this section as `## Detailed Design`; the design standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. These are the SAME required section — accept either heading and never rewrite one into the other.
- Formulas must include variable definitions, expected value ranges, and example calculations
- Edge cases must explicitly state what happens, not just "handle gracefully"
- Dependencies must be bidirectional — if system A depends on B, B's doc must mention A
- Tuning knobs must specify safe ranges and what gameplay aspect they affect
- Acceptance criteria must be testable — a QA tester must be able to verify pass/fail
- No hand-waving: "the system should feel good" is not a valid specification
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale
- Design documents MUST be written incrementally: create skeleton first, then fill
  each section one at a time with user approval between sections. Write each

# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

content.content: **SL-23 — Determinism, save-scum and wall clock.** Every persisted counter and seed is restored exactly (the kernel's `rng_derive` with counters inside the owners' blocks, G4 and D.10; the Graph keys its random draws by `(step_no, subject_id)` from `world_seed`), so the **physical** world replays the same way (Pillar 1). Whether a **perception** draw (a false system state's onset, sanity drift) replays identically after a restore, or is re-keyed, is Sanity & Hallucination Rules' decision; Save/Load makes no promise either way, and routes the constraint that any re-keying must not be steerable by the player — no reroll oracle through quit or death (OQ-37). *(Amended 2026-10-26 — CD-GDD-ALIGN)* **Threat draws and `restore_epoch` (user ruling D16, OQ-47; OQ-49 and OQ-50 closed)** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1 as amended by R13/R14)* *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R13/R14)*: Attention and Horror re-key their threat draws per restore, while the Graph's physical failures and every persisted counter and seed replay exactly (the first sentence of this paragraph stands, AC-SL-68). Resolved 2026-10-27 — delegated ruling R1, as amended 2026-10-28 by delegated rulings R13 and R14 (user delegated all remaining calls, including naming the reference machine): **Save/Load owns `restore_epoch`**, a persisted unsigned 32-bit integer that starts at 0 at `new_game` (SL-18) and is stored in the per-slot side file `slot_epoch.bin` (SL-19), so it survives a process kill, a lost `campaign.json` and a step-back. (0) *Storage (R14).* `user://saves/<campaign_id>/slot_epoch.bin` holds 8 bytes: the u32, little-endian, followed by its CRC32. The Save/Load worker writes it atomically: `slot_epoch.tmp`, flush, rename over `slot_epoch.bin`, re-read with a valid CRC32, which is the `EPOCH_DURABLE` report. It is in no generation file, so no generation's bytes, trailer SHA-256, `state_hash` or any key derived from them (SL-12's REBASED baseline key included) ever change after `VERIFYING`. Each `WORLD` generation header records the value live when that generation was written (SL-1), a read-only recovery copy that is never rewritten. The value is read once when the campaign is opened (T-6) and held in memory (`e_mem`). (1) *Advance (R13).* A death-stub restore (`DEATH_STUB`) and a `FAULT_RECOVERY` always advance `restore_epoch`. A Continue (`LOAD_GAME`, in-process or after a fresh process start) advances it unless the generation it restores is a `QUIT` generation that is the newest non-demoted verified generation: that Continue **carries the epoch unchanged** and writes nothing, so a Save & Quit followed by Continue replays the identical threat draws (user ruling D16, "not steerable by quit", outranks R1). A Continue of any other generation (an `AUTO` or `EVENT` generation after a kill or crash, or an older generation reached by fallback) advances it. An advance sets `restore_epoch := min(2^32 − 1, max(e_mem, e_slot) + 1)`, `e_slot` the value last read from `slot_epoch.bin`; at 2^32 − 1 it saturates and logs. A step-back, a demotion, a quarantine or a lost manifest cannot lower it. A stub that finds nothing loadable (`SL_LOAD_NO_LOADABLE_SAVE`) restores nothing and does not advance it. (2) *Durable before the restore is requested (R14).* When an advance is due, Save/Load runs a pre-restore staging step: after selection, pre-check and staging (SL-8, SL-11) it computes the new value and hands the `slot_epoch.bin` write to the worker as its own job, never queued behind a generation write or an abandoned job (SL-10). It polls the job once per frame, never blocking the main thread, and calls `request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash)` only after `EPOCH_DURABLE`, so the kernel's `LOADING` holds no wait on Save/Load I/O and stays atomic within one boundary service (kernel CR-15). *Staging interval (`t_epoch_wait`, F-8).* On the death stub the kernel stays `RUNNING` from the `DEAD` boundary to the boundary at which `request_restore` is made: normally one frame, at most `RESTORE_EPOCH_WRITE_MAX_MS` (30 frames at 60 Hz). During it the seat stays `DEAD`, the hard gate is closed (a seat `DEAD`, a restore pending), and a `restore_pending` latch refuses every capture and pause request of Save/Load's (the dead world is never saved, SL-7) and answers further restore triggers with `SL_LOAD_REENTRANT`. The staged payload is immutable, so nothing ticked in the interval reaches the restored world except `PROFILE`-scoped writes (Pillar 5), and the Presenter holds the down sheet's last frame. For a Continue the staging runs behind the Continue press, before the kernel is touched; a carried Continue has no staging interval. (2a) *Failure path, a listed exposure.* If the write fails, or `RESTORE_EPOCH_WRITE_MAX_MS` (placeholder 500, a monotonic I/O timeout) passes without `EPOCH_DURABLE`, Save/Load still calls `request_restore` with the advanced value held in memory, logs `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` and sets `save_status = FAILED`, because the device is failing and saving is impossible anyway. The worker re-attempts the `slot_epoch.bin` write with the next write job, and after every later `WRITTEN` generation Save/Load rewrites `slot_epoch.bin` whenever the in-memory value is ahead of the file. A kill before a later successful write may replay that epoch once (OQ-25). (2b) *Recovery copy.* A missing `slot_epoch.bin`, or one failing its CRC32, reads as `max(the newest verified generation's header copy, 0) + 1`, logs `SL_EPOCH_FILE_REBUILT` and is rewritten by the worker; a leftover `slot_epoch.tmp` is deleted (T-6). Deleting the side file by hand therefore re-keys the next stretch once, a tampering exposure of the same class as editing any save file (OQ-25). (3) *Reach into the sim.* `request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash)` hands the value to the kernel, which exposes it read-only, sim-visible and pure in `kernel.clock` as `(T, world_seed, restore_epoch)` before the first `restore()`. The kernel owns the one derivation for threat draws, `counter_eff = rng_counter + RESTORE_KEY_STRIDE × restore_epoch` (`RESTORE_KEY_STRIDE` 1 048 576, owned by the kernel; the stream-name hash stays cached and unchanged); Attention and Horror call that derivation and define none of their own, and the name `threat_epoch()` is retired in favour of `restore_epoch`. The Graph's physical failures and every persisted counter never read it. (4) *Determinism is defined given the pair:* the same (save bytes, `restore_epoch`) replays identically, and tests pin the epoch (AC-SL-142, AC-SL-145). (5) *What it prices, stated plainly:* the player can neither pick nor predict the new value; a death re-keys the next stretch (the price, metric M2); a Save & Quit followed by Continue carries the epoch (R13), so the threat draws after it are those an uninterrupted run would meet and quit buys nothing (metric M3 measures only the disguised manual save); a kill then Continue of an `AUTO` or `EVENT` generation advances it, priced by the minutes lost since that autosave (OQ-25). A kill after a carried Continue, followed by a second Continue of the same `QUIT` generation, also carries the epoch and replays that stretch exactly, a repeat and not a re-key, an accepted exposure of the same kind as OQ-25's kill. History: the rule "advances on a death-stub restore only" and R1's rule "advances on every restore" are superseded by (1) (R13), and R1's header rewrite of the restored generation and its end-of-`LOADING` wait by (0) and (2) (R14). Save/Load stores true SIM state only (SL-24). Every interval, gap and window in SL-4, SL-5 and SL-8 is in ticks read from `kernel.clock.T`; `created_unix` and `game_version` are file metadata written by the service and never read by the sim (H9), so the tests are deterministic. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **Wall clock, and the one exception.** The wall clock is never read in a decision about sim time. `SAVE_QUIT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `RENAME_RETRY_DELAY_MS`, `READ_RETRY_DELAY_MS` and `DEATH_STUB_WRITE_WAIT_MS` are millisecond **I/O timeouts** that must run while `T` is frozen (`PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `LOADING`), so they read the engine's **monotonic** millisecond counter through an injected source; a timeout never changes sim state, schedules an autosave or enters a gate input. `RESTORE_EPOCH_WRITE_MAX_MS` is the fifth monotonic I/O timeout and the one that runs while `T` advances (the death stub's dead-world staging interval, (2)); it reads the same source and changes no sim state *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R14)*. The Graph's note that "single-slot autosave is Save/Load's and the user's decision" is answered by SL-3's ring; the determinism argument is unaffected. The kernel's `rng_derive` note that a 63-bit owner-defined key is a valid `counter` appears only in OQ-3 as a routed kernel amendment (D.10), not as a rule here. A process kill after a mistake rewinds by at most one interval plus the deferral cap — the same price as dying, minus the death floor — and is an accepted, unpreventable exposure (no write can protect against it), recorded for playtest.

### F-5. `write_budget`

The `write_budget` formula is defined as:

`main_added_ms = t_file_encode + t_handoff; main_hitch_ms = capture_time_ms + main_added_ms; worker_ms = t_sha + t_write + t_flush + t_reread + t_resha + t_swap + t_manifest; durable_ms = main_hitch_ms + worker_ms; checks: main_hitch_ms ≤ SNAPSHOT_BUDGET_MS, t_handoff ≤ WRITE_HANDOFF_MAX_FRACTION × SNAPSHOT_BUDGET_MS, t_file_encode ≤ SAVE_ENCODE_BUDGET_MS, durable_ms ≤ WRITE_DURABLE_ALARM_MS, worker_ms ≤ DOWN_TO_DEATH_TICKS × 1000 / TICK_RATE (logging only); a job past WRITE_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS is abandoned (SL-10)` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*

**Variables:**

| Variable | Type | Range | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `capture_time_ms` | float ms | within `SNAPSHOT_BUDGET_MS` (kernel GDD value 16.7, logging threshold only) | kernel D.11 (cited; Save/Load neither restates nor adds to it) | Σ `t_snapshot(b)` + `t_hash` inside `SAVING`; with the stored `state_hash`, the hash is a release cost on every capture (OQ-17). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* `t_hash` is a main-thread cost: ≈ 1.5 ms [UNV, spike AC-SL-89] for the ratified native H64 (truncated SHA-256); a scripted xxHash64 or FNV-1a loop would be 15 … 150 ms [UNV] and is not used; release builds pay `t_hash` as well (K-4 adopted, SL-16; the example's 1.5 ms already budgets it, so no F-5 number changes) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* |
| `t_file_encode`, `t_handoff` | float ms | 0 … ~10 [UNV]; 0 … ~2 | Save/Load, main thread, tick halted | Per-block `var_to_bytes` of the captured plain data only; moving the blocks to the worker. The SHA work, header and trailer are worker work (T-4); `t_file_encode` is Save/Load's term and is not the kernel's `t_encode(b)` (D.11, OQ-53) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* |
| `t_sha`, `t_resha` | float ms | ~0.3 … 2 at 60–300 KiB [UNV] | worker, native hashing | Per-block `payload_sha256`, header assembly and the trailer SHA-256 at write (moved off the main thread, *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*), and the verify re-read |
| `t_write`, `t_flush`, `t_reread` | float ms | 2 … 100 (AV and indexers add 50 … 500) [UNV] | worker | Disk dependent |
| `t_swap`, `t_manifest` | float ms | 1 … 20 [UNV] | worker | The two renames of the swap, `POST_VERIFY`, and the manifest rewrite |
| `WRITE_HANDOFF_MAX_FRACTION` | float | 0.01 … 0.2, default 0.05 | Tuning Knobs | Share of `SNAPSHOT_BUDGET_MS` the hand-off may take |
| `SAVE_ENCODE_BUDGET_MS`, `WRITE_DURABLE_ALARM_MS` | float ms | 2 … 16, default 4; 200 … 2 000, default 500 | Tuning Knobs | Logging thresholds, never truncating |
| `DOWN_TO_DEATH_TICKS` | int | 1 800 (registry, cited) | Controller | A write that settles inside the `DOWNED` window cannot race a death on the timer path; after a solo `give_up` the window is only `GIVE_UP_MIN_TICKS`, and a job still busy then is abandoned (SL-7) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)* |

**Output Range:** `main_hitch_ms`, the main-thread sum, is the quantity the player can feel as a stutter, and a stutter that appears only on writes is itself a Pillar 3 leak: it tells the player when the game saved and when the gate deferred, the signal UI-1 was retired for. The check `main_hitch_ms ≤ SNAPSHOT_BUDGET_MS` therefore gates the hash choice (SL-16), and `main_added_ms` adds to — is not part of — the kernel's capture *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. `worker_ms` is bounded in effect, not in principle: a job that has not settled `DEATH_STUB_WRITE_WAIT_MS` after `DOWNED` entry, or is still busy at `DEAD`, is abandoned (SL-10), so stuck I/O costs a stale file and not a stuck game. The 30 000 ms logging ceiling is `1 800 × 1 000 / 60` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. All components are [UNV] estimates the spike replaces; every threshold logs and none truncates.

**Example (MVP slice: 14 blocks, 86 016 B payload, SSD, native truncated SHA-256)** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: `capture_time_ms = 4.6` (Graph 0.5 + thirteen small blocks at 0.2 = 3.1 of snapshots, plus a 1.5 hash), `t_file_encode = 2.0`, `t_handoff = 0.3` (≤ 0.05 × 16.7 = 0.835 ✓): `main_hitch_ms = 6.9 ≤ 16.7` ✓. `worker_ms = 0.3 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 0.3 + 4 + 3 = 15.6`; `durable_ms = 22.5 ≤ 500` ✓. A slow HDD with a scanner: `worker_ms = 300`, `durable_ms = 306.9` ✓, and the job settles far inside `DEATH_STUB_WRITE_WAIT_MS`. **Scripted-hash counter-example:** with `hash_algo` 0 or 1 as a per-byte loop at 15 … 150 ms [UNV], `capture_time_ms` becomes 18.1 … 153.1 and `main_hitch_ms` 20.4 … 155.4, which fails `main_hitch_ms ≤ SNAPSHOT_BUDGET_MS`; that is why the ratified H64 is native (SL-16, R-17); release builds pay the capture-time hash too, now that K-4 gives it a consumer *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*.

**SL-16 — Hash roles (D8; R10, R15).** Four distinct integrity layers, no overlap. (1) The **file trailer** SHA-256 over every preceding byte and (2) the per-block **`payload_sha256`** over each stored payload — Save/Load's own, fixed, native [UNV], verified before the kernel is touched; they localise damage and guard accidental corruption and truncation, not tampering. (3) The header **`state_hash`** and the optional per-block **`block_state_hash`** are the *kernel's* 64-bit hash over the owners' canonical bytes (D.12), named by `hash_algo`, so the ratified hash (H64 = first 8 bytes, little-endian, of SHA-256 via `HashingContext`, `hash_algo` 2; R-17, user ruling X13, registry `state_hash`) and the per-block cached hash (**K-1**, a kernel ADR candidate — cited, never owned) can change with no `format_version` bump *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings, consistency follow-up)*; `block_state_hash` is present only if the kernel exposes a per-block hash, is diagnostic and is never a refusal reason. (4) The post-restore **reproduction compare** of SL-12 detects a restore that does not reproduce the snapshot — a bug, not corruption. The kernel's D.11 worked example assumed the hash cost is a debug-build cost; this design makes it a release cost on every capture and restore, and the ratified H64 is native, so the remaining cost question is whether SHA-256 over 100–300 KiB stays near the 1.5 ms that example allowed [UNV] — the spike (AC-SL-89) measures it, and K-1 is the mitigation if it does not (OQ-2, OQ-17) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings, consistency follow-up)*. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Godot's `HashingContext` offers only MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 [UNV: 4.5 – 4.7 are post-cutoff, confirm in the spike], so a scripted `hash_algo` 0 (xxHash64) or 1 (FNV-1a 64) would be a per-byte loop, estimated at 15 to 150 ms over ~90 KiB (the range between the first review and the game-designer's estimate) [UNV]; a hitch that appears only on writes would tell the player when the game saved, the signal UI-1 was retired for. **Ratified** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings, consistency follow-up)*: the default is the **native truncated SHA-256** (`hash_algo` 2, H64), which `HashingContext` computes natively (R-17, user ruling X13). With K-4 adopted (kernel CR-15) the capture-time `state_hash` has a release consumer and is written in every build (SL-1) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*.

**SL-13 — Observation channel for a control-plane caller (provisional — kernel owner).** Save/Load is a host-local control-plane caller (CR-15), not one of the kernel's five subscriber classes (PRESENTATION, INPUT_SURFACE, PROJECTOR, REPLICATION, DIAGNOSTIC). Its reads are limited to: `kernel.clock` (`T`, `world_seed`); `controller.state.loco_state` per bound seat (its `DOWNED` → non-`DOWNED` transitions give the refractory's `last_recover_T`, SL-5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)*; the Life-Support Graph's `read_view.failures()` for the Graph half of the soft gate (designed, LS-19; required at MVP; a SIM read with no perceived variant, so it is not a `PERCEPTION_OUT` view) and the optional Attention SIM view `attention.view` for the Attention half (designed; absent = open); Suit's `view(player_id).vitals_state` per bound seat for the critical-suit input (designed, SE-33, a SIM read) and Assembly's pure read `ragged_breach_open()` for the open-breach input (registered, source Modular Ship Assembly) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings, consistency follow-up)*; the event-trigger reads of SL-4 (the `POD_ARRIVED` notification, Assembly's pure read `last_shape_change_T()` and Interaction's pure read `last_salvage_T()`); and the Controller's end-of-tick change notification for `controller.state` (for the death stub) and for any PROFILE block (for SL-9). It **never** reads a `PERCEPTION_OUT` view (CR-12, H5) and **never writes a block** (H3, H4). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1)* It reads no epoch: `restore_epoch` is Save/Load's own persisted value (SL-23) and reaches the sim as an argument of `request_restore`, never as a read. Which subscriber class or read access a persistence service has is not stated by the kernel's interaction table; it is routed to the kernel owner (OQ-7), and until it is answered every observation is a tick-boundary read-view poll made in the same boundary in which the request will be issued.
**SL-17 — Zero blocks, zero hooks (D13).** Save/Load registers no state block and no step hook: ring bookkeeping lives in `campaign.json`, because a WORLD block would roll back on restore and desync the file set from the world. The kernel's acceptance criterion that the registry holds exactly one block, `kernel.clock`, stays true with Save/Load booted. The MVP save request is a host-local API call (CR-15), so CR-16's "save-request state" is not needed. A `saveload.request_save` command type (`origin PLAYER`, `allowed_when_paused`, `actor_binding NONE`) for VS-B guests is **reserved and (provisional — Co-op Session & Replication, VS-B)** at every mention; nothing in the MVP depends on it.
